target.title: Real-time synthesis of imagined speech processes from minimally invasive recordings of neural activity

read.pdf: Fig. 1–6 captions and Table 1 as present in text.txt; no separate PDF inspected

entries.text: The 40-bin LDA decoder was trained on the first open-loop run with audible, articulated speech and then applied without retraining during whispered and imagined closed-loop runs.
entries.condition: One participant; open-loop audible run used as training data; two subsequent feedback runs used whisper and instructed imagery.

entries.text: The authors frame prior speech synthesis work as offline/open-loop and based on articulated or mimed speech, leaving real-time decoding of imagined speech as an unresolved challenge.
entries.condition: Authors' literature framing; see also the separate real-time and imagined-speech studies below.

entries.text: The authors say Moses et al. decoded speech to text in real time but used produced or perceived speech rather than imagined speech.
entries.condition: Prior studies as characterized by the target paper.

entries.text: The authors say Martin et al. studied imagined speech offline on open-loop data.
entries.condition: Prior studies as characterized by the target paper.

entries.text: The paper identifies an earlier real-time imagined-speech-related synthesis study, but says it only synthesized basic vowel sounds.
entries.condition: The earlier study is the paper's cited reference 16, a patient with a neurotrophic motor-cortex electrode.

entries.text: The stated novelty is real-time synthesis of imagined spoken words from neural recordings, addressing the two open challenges identified by the authors.
entries.condition: Single-participant proof of concept; prompted words; model trained on the participant's audible speech.
entries.quote: Here, we show the feasibility of real-time synthesis of imagined spoken words from neural recordings, thereby directly addressing the two open challenges in the development of speech neuroprosthetics.

entries.text: The experiment involved one participant, a 20-year-old woman.
entries.condition: Single female patient with severe epilepsy; native Dutch speaker; all training and closed-loop conditions used this participant.

entries.text: The participant had 11 sEEG shafts containing 119 contacts, predominantly in the left hemisphere.
entries.condition: One patient's clinically placed sEEG electrodes; contacts predominantly in left frontal and lateral areas.
entries.loc: Anatomical and temporal contributions; Methods: Participant

entries.text: Each sEEG electrode was 0.8 mm in diameter and contained 8–18 contacts; contacts were 2 mm long with 1.5 mm inter-contact spacing.
entries.unit: mm diameter; contacts per electrode; mm contact length; mm spacing
entries.condition: Implanted platinum-iridium Microdeep sEEG electrodes used for the single-participant study.

entries.text: Neural data were recorded on a 128-channel amplifier at 2048 Hz; microphone audio was recorded at 48 kHz.
entries.condition: One participant; sEEG referenced to a common white-matter electrode; neural and audio streams synchronized by LabStreamingLayer.

entries.text: Each run prompted 100 Dutch words from a phonetically balanced 250-word list; each word appeared for 2 s followed by a 1-s intertrial interval, yielding about 5 min per run.
entries.unit: words per run; words in list; seconds per prompt; seconds intertrial; minutes per run
entries.condition: Three sequential runs: audible open-loop training, whispered feedback, and imagined-speech feedback; vocabulary drawn from IFA words and numbers 1–10.

entries.text: High-gamma features used a 70–170 Hz band and order-8 filters to attenuate the 50-Hz line-noise harmonics.
entries.unit: Hz band; filter order; Hz line noise
entries.condition: sEEG preprocessing for the single participant; first and second line-noise harmonics attenuated with two notch filters.

entries.text: Neural features used 50-ms windows with 10-ms shifts, natural-log power, and past context extending to −200 ms; future context was excluded.
entries.unit: ms window; ms frame shift; ms past context
entries.condition: Causal real-time feature extraction; five temporal contexts from −200 to 0 ms are described in the anatomical analysis.
entries.quote: The resulting signals were segmented into 50 ms windows with a 10 ms frameshift to capture the complex dynamics of speech processes.

entries.text: Audio targets were 40 logarithmic mel coefficients from audio downsampled to 16 kHz, using 16-ms windows and 10-ms shifts.
entries.unit: coefficients; Hz; ms window; ms frame shift
entries.condition: Time-aligned microphone speech recordings used as training labels and reference spectrograms.
entries.quote: This preprocessing procedure aligned sEEG features and spectral acoustic features while preserving speech-relevant information, and results for each window in 40 logarithmic mel-scaled spectral coefficients.

entries.text: Each of the 40 spectral bins was quantized to nine energy classes using logistic intervals with growth-rate k = 0.5.
entries.unit: spectral bins; classes per bin; logistic growth-rate k
entries.condition: Quantization of log-mel acoustic training targets; classes represent spectral-bin energy levels, including silence.
entries.loc: Methods: Audio signal processing; Methods: Classification approach

entries.text: The decoder comprised 40 regularized LDA classifiers and used the 150 features most correlated with speech energy.
entries.condition: One classifier predicts one energy class for each mel bin; features selected on training data; models trained on audible open-loop data.
entries.quote: Thus, the system consists of 40 LDA-classifiers that are trained on the open-loop data from the first experimental run.

entries.text: The authors selected bounded class outputs to keep synthesized output within typical speech-production boundaries and to increase robustness to neural noise and outliers.
entries.condition: Simple LDA classification of discretized acoustic energy rather than unbounded regression.

entries.text: The spectrogram-to-waveform stage used eight Griffin–Lim reconstruction iterations.
entries.condition: Audible waveform generated continuously from decoded mel spectrograms and played as real-time auditory feedback.

entries.text: The system continuously generated an auditory waveform without an explicit speech/silence-onset detector; intended speech-pattern activity should produce sound and other activity silence.
entries.condition: Closed-loop sEEG decoder with continuous acoustic feedback; no word-level output or explicit onset-detection stage.

entries.text: The audible open-loop evaluation used ten-fold cross-validation over the entire run, including trials and intertrial intervals.
entries.condition: Retrospective evaluation on the same single-participant open-loop run used to train closed-loop models; metric was average Pearson correlation across frequency bins.

entries.text: Open-loop time-aligned reconstruction achieved average Pearson correlation 0.62 ± 0.15 across spectral bins.
entries.condition: Ten-fold cross-validation on the complete audible open-loop run, including trials and intertrial intervals; one participant; 40 mel bins; time-aligned reference; LDA decoder trained within folds.

entries.text: The five visually selected highest-scoring examples had correlation 0.89 for the left example and 0.82 for each of the other examples.
entries.condition: Examples selected from open-loop reconstruction by highest Pearson-correlation scores; illustrative, not an unselected test average.

entries.text: The open-loop chance baseline was created by randomly splitting and swapping the acoustic data's temporal partitions, retraining the complete decoding pipeline on the broken alignment.
entries.condition: Audible open-loop baseline; temporal neural/audio correspondence deliberately broken; not a held-out participant or random-label benchmark.

entries.text: Open-loop randomized-alignment chance remained around Pearson r = 0.1; the null procedure was repeated 100 times.
entries.condition: Open-loop run; each chance rerun retrained the pipeline after breaking temporal audio/neural alignment; one participant and 40 bins.

entries.text: Open-loop scores exceeded the randomized baseline in every frequency bin (Mann–Whitney U, P < 0.001; n1 = 10, n2 = 100; Bonferroni corrected).
entries.condition: Per-frequency comparisons of open-loop fold scores with 100 broken-alignment baseline reruns; Bonferroni correction across frequency bins.

entries.text: The authors state reconstructed speech is not intelligible and use correlation instead of STOI/ESTOI because some trials may not contain 400 ms of consecutive speech.
entries.unit: ms consecutive speech assumed by STOI/ESTOI
entries.condition: Open-loop performance metric; correlations measure spectrogram similarity, not word intelligibility.
entries.quote: Currently, reconstructed speech is not intelligible.

entries.text: Mean per-node processing costs were 0.137 ms (channel selection), 0.773 (high-gamma), 0.766 (noise filtering), 0.597 (log power), 0.406 (context buffering), 0.379 (context stacking), 2.008 (decoding), 0.612 (dequantization), and 1.652 (Griffin–Lim); total 7.331 ms.
entries.unit: ms per node; total ms per 10 ms neural input
entries.condition: Mean processing times on the research laptop; one process for the decoding pipeline; values are the Table 1 per-node timings.
entries.quote: In total, for 10 ms of neural signals, 7.3 ms are needed for the conversion into an acoustic signal.

entries.text: For VAD evaluation, authors report energy threshold 4, mean scaling 0.5, up to five context frames on each side, and 60% required speech-frame proportion.
entries.unit: threshold; scale; context frames per side; percent
entries.condition: Kaldi-style energy VAD applied to decoded audio; hyperparameters chosen using training audio and then applied for evaluation.
entries.quote: We used an energy threshold of 4 with a mean scaling of 0.5.

entries.text: Figure 4 displays five selected synthesized waveform examples for each closed-loop condition.
entries.condition: Illustrative whispered and imagined trials; not the complete evaluation set.

entries.text: Whispered-condition reference comparisons used 73 words shared between the open-loop and whispered runs; the patient's whisper was below microphone sensitivity, so no direct whispered reference was available.
entries.condition: Same participant and prompted vocabulary; open-loop audible articulation served as reference; trials were not precisely time-aligned and were aligned by DTW.

entries.text: Closed-loop chance references came from randomly selected 2-s sEEG segments recorded during a separate nonspeech session involving grasping and eye fixation; 1000 samples were generated.
entries.condition: One participant; neural data from nonspeech task session; decoded segments compared by DTW with reference articulations.
entries.quote: This procedure was repeated 1000 times to create a reliable distribution.

entries.text: Whispered closed-loop matched-word trials had median DTW correlation 0.64 ± 0.15.
entries.condition: n=73 whispered trials with words overlapping the audible open-loop run; single participant; audible open-loop articulations used as time-warped references; chance decoder used 2-s nonspeech sEEG segments; no language model.
entries.quote: Our approach achieved median DTW correlations of 0.64 ± 0.15 and 0.17 ± 0.23 for the chance level (Fig. 4c).

entries.text: Whispered-condition chance DTW correlation was 0.17 ± 0.23.
entries.condition: 1000 randomly selected 2-s nonspeech sEEG segments from grasping/eye-fixation activity; reference word articulation drawn from the audible training run; one participant.

entries.text: Whispered scores were significantly above the chance distribution (Mann–Whitney U, P < 0.001; n1 = 73, n2 = 1000).
entries.condition: DTW-aligned spectrogram correlations; same participant; two-sided Mann–Whitney U test per Methods.
entries.loc: Results: whispered; Methods: Statistics and reproducibility

entries.text: The VAD analysis found synthesized speech during most whispered trials and little decoded speech in speechless intervals.
entries.condition: Qualitative VAD result in Fig. 4d; article does not give exact proportions in the text.

entries.text: Because microphone audio did not provide a whispered reference, the reported whispered score compares to the participant's audible articulations for matching prompted words after optimal DTW alignment.
entries.condition: The 73 shared words were not precisely time-aligned across the open-loop and whispered runs; DTW maximizes temporal correspondence.

entries.text: The imagined-speech run shared 75 prompted words with the audible open-loop run for reference comparison.
entries.condition: Same single participant and vocabulary; open-loop audible reference articulation; imagined decoder trained on the audible open-loop run and evaluated by DTW.
entries.quote: For this case, 75 random words overlapped with the open-loop run.

entries.text: Imagined-speech matched-word evaluation reported mean DTW correlation 0.32 ± 0.26.
entries.condition: n=75 imagined trials sharing prompts with the audible open-loop run; same participant; audible references optimally time-warped; 40 mel bins; no language model.
entries.quote: We achieve mean correlation coefficients of 0.32 ± 0.26 for our proposed method, which is significantly higher than the chance level of 0.17 ± 0.22

entries.text: Imagined-condition chance DTW correlation was 0.17 ± 0.22.
entries.condition: 1000 randomly selected 2-s nonspeech sEEG segments from the participant's grasping/eye-fixation activity; reference word articulation from audible open-loop run.
entries.quote: We achieve mean correlation coefficients of 0.32 ± 0.26 for our proposed method, which is significantly higher than the chance level of 0.17 ± 0.22

entries.text: Imagined-speech scores exceeded chance (Mann–Whitney U, P < 0.01; n1 = 75, n2 = 1000).
entries.condition: DTW-aligned correlations; one participant; two-sided Mann–Whitney U test per Methods.
entries.loc: Results: imagined; Methods: Statistics and reproducibility

entries.text: Imagined-speech decoding was significantly lower than whispered-speech decoding (Mann–Whitney U, P < 0.001; n1 = 75, n2 = 73).
entries.condition: Comparison of DTW correlations for matching prompted words in the same participant; two-sided Mann–Whitney U test per Methods.
entries.loc: Results: imagined; Methods: Statistics and reproducibility

entries.text: VAD-marked speech occurred during most imagined trials, but more speech segments also appeared in nonspeech intervals than in the whispered run.
entries.condition: Qualitative VAD output for instructed imagery and intertrial intervals; no exact proportions stated in article text.
entries.quote: The majority of speech segments as identified by VAD still occurred during the imagined trials (Fig. 4d)

entries.text: The authors attribute some imagined-condition intertrial speech detections to uncertainty about the participant's internal performance and differences between imagined and overt speech processes.
entries.condition: Proposed explanation for increased nonspeech-interval VAD detections; not a separately measured cause.

entries.text: The authors interpret successful cross-mode decoding as evidence that audible, whispered, and imagined speech share some neural representations, permitting transfer of the audible-trained model.
entries.condition: Single participant; model trained on audible speech and transferred to whisper and imagined-speech runs; the result is a decoder-transfer finding, not proof of identical neural processes.

entries.text: Anatomical analysis used five temporal contexts from −200 to 0 ms; the decoder relied most on high-gamma activity 150–200 ms before the current time point.
entries.unit: contexts; ms lag range; ms strongest lag
entries.condition: Selected features and Haufe-transformed LDA activations from the audible open-loop run; activations averaged over 9 classes and 40 frequency bins.

entries.text: The authors report dominant inferior/middle frontal contributions, with some central/postcentral activity, and interpret the pattern as shared speech-planning and execution activity across vocalized, whispered, and imagined modes.
entries.condition: Activation maps from one participant and one audible open-loop training run; not an independently validated anatomical biomarker.
entries.loc: Fig. 5; Results: Anatomical and temporal contributions

entries.text: The authors argue sEEG may support long-term implantation with less surgical trauma than other intracranial modalities and compare its electrodes to DBS systems.
entries.condition: Discussion-level translational rationale; this experiment did not test chronic implantation or a patient cohort.

entries.text: The current decoder still requires audible speech from the patient for model training; the authors suggest early implantation or surrogate imagined-speech data as possible future routes.
entries.condition: Current reported model was trained on this participant's audible open-loop speech; suggested alternatives were not evaluated.

entries.text: Authors concede the synthesized speech was not intelligible and had inferior quality to prior offline decoding of audible and whispered speech.
entries.condition: Qualitative output-quality limitation; the reported study establishes gated acoustic output, not intelligible communication.

entries.text: Only individual prompted words were tested; spontaneous speech needed for natural conversation remains untested.
entries.condition: One prompted-word task with three 100-word runs; no spontaneous or continuous sentence production evaluation.

entries.text: The authors characterize these findings as initial proof-of-concept evidence from one patient, rather than a demonstrated practical neuroprosthesis for a population.
entries.condition: Single 20-year-old female patient with epilepsy; no between-participant or subject-independent evaluation.

entries.text: The authors say causal real-time decoding did not rely on perceived auditory feedback and therefore reflected neural processes underlying speech production.
entries.condition: Closed-loop whisper/imagination runs with system feedback; claimed causal design, in one participant.
entries.quote: Based on our causal design, the decoding results do not rely on perceived auditory feedback of vocalizations and are based on neural processes underlying speech production.

entries.text: The paper describes spectral-bin classification and waveform reconstruction but does not specify a use-time language model, lexicon, or word-level constraint.
entries.condition: The output is an acoustic spectrogram/waveform, not a textual word prediction; no linguistic aid is described.

entries.text: No separate user confirmation or accept/reject mechanism is specified; the reported feedback is continuous audio.
entries.condition: Closed-loop task as described; no confirmation stage between decoded output and auditory presentation.

entries.text: No explicit correction interface or discrete edit operation is specified; authors discuss future user learning and co-adaptation instead.
entries.condition: The user receives continuous auditory feedback and is instructed to whisper or imagine prompted words; no correction control is reported.

entries.text: The paper reports randomization repetitions but no random seed or random-state setting for the fold baseline, chance segments, or other stochastic analyses.
entries.condition: Reproducibility condition; chance procedures are described as random but no seed is reported in the paper.

entries.text: Beyond logarithmic high-gamma power and feature-windowing, the paper does not specify a z-score or other standardization of neural feature channels before LDA.
entries.condition: Training and decoding feature scaling; paper specifies the natural-log power transform but not channel-wise centering/scaling.

entries.text: The paper reports Griffin–Lim iteration count but not its normalization/norm factor.
entries.condition: Waveform reconstruction setting needed to reproduce amplitude/normalization; code configuration provides a value.

entries.text: The paper does not state whether closed-loop significance tests were adjusted for multiple comparisons; it explicitly reports Bonferroni correction only for the open-loop per-frequency analysis.
entries.condition: Three closed-loop comparisons are reported: whisper vs chance, imagined vs chance, and imagined vs whisper.

entries.text: Executable exp1.py uses KFold(n_splits=10) without shuffling; each test fold is a contiguous word block, held out from its first word through 3 seconds after its last word, and models are fit on the remaining data.

questions.q: Was the decoder trained on imagined speech, and what does its transfer result establish?
questions.answer: No. It was trained on audible open-loop speech and transferred to whispered and imagined runs in the same participant. This supports feasibility of cross-mode acoustic decoding in that participant, not word recognition or population-level generalization.

questions.q: Does the reported evidence show intelligible imagined-word communication?
questions.answer: No. The output is explicitly reported as not yet intelligible; the task tested individual prompted words and evaluated spectrogram similarity after DTW alignment, not decoded word identity.

questions.q: Can the open-loop correlation be directly compared with the whispered or imagined scores?
questions.answer: No. Open-loop references are time-aligned, whereas the closed-loop scores use DTW to optimize temporal alignment; the paper explicitly says these correlations are not directly comparable.

questions.q: What evaluation details affect exact reproducibility or interpretation?
questions.answer: The repository uses non-shuffled contiguous word folds, does not set random seeds, adds audio scaling/noise, specifies Griffin–Lim norm 10, and differs from the paper's VAD settings; its open-loop significance code also pools fold-wise chance scores differently from the reported n2.

questions.q: (writer, answered from targeted passages in the named papers) Which prior studies closed the loop with audio playback, and did the group's earlier offline study use a listener or identification test?
questions.answer: Closed loop with playback: Guenther 2009 (intracortical), Berry 2014 and Bocquelet 2015/2016 (EMA), Brumberg 2018 (EEG); Gilbert 2017 simulated causal delays offline; Janke 2017 and Hofe 2011 report real-time capability without a closed-loop run. Herff 2019 used a four-option forced-choice listening test with 55 listeners (66.1% vs 25% chance).
